```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE)
sbc <- read.csv("validation-sbc.csv", check.names = FALSE)
mc <- read.csv("validation-mc.csv", check.names = FALSE)
bench <- read.csv("validation-bench.csv", check.names = FALSE)
cuts <- read.csv("validation-cutpoints.csv", check.names = FALSE)
bins <- as.matrix(sbc[, paste0("b", 1:10)])
```

An MCMC sampler can run, produce plausible numbers and still be wrong: a
conditional distribution off by a term, a block order that breaks a collapsed
Gibbs step, a move that does not preserve the target. Such errors bias the
posterior without any error message. This vignette summarises the evidence
that the samplers in `panelspatialprobit` target the right posterior and that
the resulting estimates behave as they should. The scripts and full results
are in the `validation/` directory of the source repository; the figures below
are drawn from summaries of those results stored with this vignette.

The evidence comes in four layers:

1. **an independent reference sampler** in the test suite;
2. **simulation-based calibration** of every model variant;
3. **a Monte Carlo study** of bias and coverage;
4. **cross-checks** against other packages.

A last section reports the speed and mixing of the sampler.

## 1. An independent reference sampler

The package contains a second sampler written in plain R that deliberately
uses different algorithms: dense precision matrices instead of the sparse
residual updates, random-walk Metropolis steps with exact log-determinants for
$\rho$, $\lambda$, $\phi$ and the latent AR coefficient instead of griddy
Gibbs steps, and no scale or cut-point moves. It shares no sampling code with
the Rust engine. The test suite runs both on the same small data sets (SAR,
SEM, SARAR, spatial random effects, Student-t errors, time-varying weights,
latent dynamics, binary and ordered) and requires every posterior mean to agree
within four Monte Carlo standard errors. A mistake in one sampler
would have to be repeated, through a different route, in the other.

The cut-point moves are tested separately: started from draws of a known
joint distribution, one step of the kernel must leave that distribution
unchanged.

## 2. Simulation-based calibration

Simulation-based calibration (SBC; Talts et al. 2018) checks a sampler
against its own model. Draw parameters from the prior, simulate a data set
from them, fit the model, and record the rank of the true value among the
posterior draws. If the sampler targets the correct posterior, these ranks are
uniformly distributed, whatever the data. A sampler that is too confident
gives U-shaped rank histograms; one that is biased gives skewed ones.

The design: a 4 × 4 rook grid ($N = 16$), $T = 4$ periods, proper priors
($\beta \sim N(0, 1)$, $(\rho + 1)/2 \sim \text{Beta}(2, 2)$, the same for
$\lambda$ and $\phi$, $\sigma_\alpha^2 \sim \text{Inv-Gamma}(3, 1)$,
cut-points $\sim N(1, 1)$), 500 replications per variant, two chains, 400
thinned posterior draws per fit. Uniformity of each parameter's ranks is tested
by a chi-square test on 10 bins.

```{r}
runs <- unique(sbc[, c("variant", "seed_offset")])
```

In all, `r nrow(runs)` runs of `r length(unique(sbc$variant))` variants were
made, with `r nrow(sbc)` rank tests. Under correct calibration the p-values of
these tests are themselves uniform: about 5% should fall below 0.05 and 1%
below 0.01 by chance alone.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Histogram and uniform quantile plot of SBC p-values"}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex = 0.8)
hist(sbc$p, breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05), main = "SBC p-values", xlab = "chi-square p-value",
     col = "grey80", border = "white")
abline(h = nrow(sbc) / 20, lty = 2)
latent_default <- sbc$variant == "sar_lat_re_bin"
plot(ppoints(nrow(sbc)), sort(sbc$p), pch = 19, cex = 0.5, xlab = "uniform quantile",
     ylab = "sorted p-value", main = "Against the uniform",
     col = ifelse(latent_default[order(sbc$p)], "firebrick", "grey30"))
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
par(op)
```

The p-values are close to uniform. Of the `r nrow(sbc)` tests,
`r sum(sbc$p < 0.05)` fall below 0.05 and `r sum(sbc$p < 0.01)` below 0.01:

```{r}
low <- sbc[sbc$p < 0.01, c("variant", "seed_offset", "parameter", "p", "median_rhat")]
knitr::kable(low, row.names = FALSE, col.names = c("variant", "seed offset", "parameter",
                                                    "p", "median max R-hat"))
```

Two come from the latent AR model with SAR at the default chain length (red
in the right panel), and the third, $\lambda$ in the SARAR model with
time-varying weights, passes in a replication with other seeds
(p = `r round(sbc$p[sbc$variant == "sarar_tv_re_ord3" & sbc$parameter == "lambda" & sbc$seed_offset == 1], 3)`).
In the latent AR model the ranks of the latent AR coefficient are
U-shaped, and the failures concentrate in the replications whose chains had
not converged (max $\hat R \geq 1.02$): the sampler mixes slowly, rather than
targeting the wrong distribution. A replication with other seeds passes
(p = `r round(sbc$p[sbc$variant == "sar_lat_re_bin" & sbc$parameter == "lag_z" & sbc$seed_offset == 1], 3)`),
and so does the same variant with chains three times as long:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.6, fig.alt = "Rank histograms of the latent AR coefficient at two chain lengths"}
rank_hist <- function(v, p, main, off = 0) {
  i <- which(sbc$variant == v & sbc$parameter == p & sbc$seed_offset == off)
  barplot(bins[i, ], names.arg = NA, space = 0, col = "grey70", border = "white",
          main = main, ylim = c(0, max(bins[i, ], 1.6 * sbc$reps[i] / 10)), cex.main = 0.9)
  abline(h = sbc$reps[i] / 10, lty = 2)
  mtext(sprintf("p = %.3f", sbc$p[i]), side = 3, line = 0, cex = 0.7)
}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 3, 3, 1), cex = 0.8)
rank_hist("sar_lat_re_bin", "lag_z", "lag_z, default chains")
rank_hist("sar_lat_re_bin_long", "lag_z", "lag_z, chains 3x as long")
par(op)
```

SARAR models with
$M = W$ show borderline results for $\rho$ and $\lambda$ at the default chain
length, again from slow mixing (the two parameters are nearly
interchangeable); this is why `?psprobit` asks for longer chains for them.

The rank histograms of a few central parameters:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.6, fig.alt = "Rank histograms for six parameters"}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(1, 3, 3, 1), cex = 0.8)
rank_hist("sar_re_bin", "rho", "SAR, binary: rho")
rank_hist("sar_re_bin", "sigma_alpha", "SAR, binary: sigma_alpha")
rank_hist("sdm_re_bin", "W_x1", "SDM, binary: W_x1")
rank_hist("sar_re_ord4", "cut[3|4]", "SAR, J = 4: cut[3|4]")
rank_hist("sem_re_bin", "lambda", "SEM, binary: lambda")
rank_hist("sar_dyn_bin", "lag_y", "Dynamic SAR: lag_y")
par(op)
```

The summary by variant (the smallest p-value over its parameters, and the
median over replications of the largest $\hat R$):

```{r}
agg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(sbc, list(sbc$variant, sbc$seed_offset), drop = TRUE),
                             function(x) data.frame(variant = x$variant[1],
                                                    seed_offset = x$seed_offset[1],
                                                    parameters = nrow(x), min_p = min(x$p),
                                                    median_rhat = x$median_rhat[1])))
agg <- agg[order(agg$variant, agg$seed_offset), ]
knitr::kable(agg, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("variant", "seed offset", "parameters", "min p",
                           "median max R-hat"))
```

Variant names give the model, the random effects (`re`: random, `pool`:
pooled, `sre`: spatial random effects, `mundlak`, `chamberlain`), the outcome
(`bin`, or `ord` with the number of categories), and any extension: `t`
(Student-t errors with 4 degrees of freedom), `tv` (time-varying weights),
`dyn` (lagged outcome with Wooldridge initial conditions), `lat` (latent AR
dynamics), `missing` (20% of outcomes missing), `ac` (Albert–Chib cut-point
sampler instead of the default transformation move), `long` (longer chains).
With several parameters per variant, the smallest p-value is naturally small;
under correct calibration it falls below 0.05 for roughly a fifth to a third
of the variants.

### The same test for `spatialprobit`

The same check, applied to `spatialprobit::sarprobit` (version 1.0.4) on a
cross-section (an 8 × 8 grid, $T = 1$, pooled SAR probit, 500 replications),
gave a clear failure. The sampler returned undefined draws in 264 of the 500
replications, and among the others the ranks of $\rho$ pile up in the top bin:
its posterior understates $\rho$. `panelspatialprobit` on the identical design
had no failures and uniform ranks:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.6, fig.alt = "Rank histograms of rho for spatialprobit and panelspatialprobit"}
sp <- c(28, 15, 14, 15, 15, 12, 19, 20, 22, 76)
psp <- c(48, 52, 63, 55, 47, 51, 53, 39, 43, 49)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 3, 3, 1), cex = 0.8)
barplot(sp, space = 0, col = "grey70", border = "white", main = "spatialprobit: rho",
        cex.main = 0.9)
abline(h = sum(sp) / 10, lty = 2)
mtext("236 successful replications, p < 0.0001", side = 3, line = 0, cex = 0.7)
barplot(psp, space = 0, col = "grey70", border = "white", main = "panelspatialprobit: rho",
        cex.main = 0.9)
abline(h = sum(psp) / 10, lty = 2)
mtext("500 replications, p = 0.550", side = 3, line = 0, cex = 0.7)
par(op)
```

Reading its source suggests three causes: the draw of $\rho$ uses the
concentrated likelihood of the linear SAR model (which integrates out an error
variance that the probit fixes at one), the block order breaks the rule for
partially collapsed Gibbs samplers, and the truncated-normal step restarts its
inner chain every iteration. Which of them causes the bias was not isolated.
Keeping only the successful replications may itself distort the ranks, so the
size of the bias is uncertain, but its presence is not.

## 3. Monte Carlo study

SBC averages over the prior. A Monte Carlo study instead fixes the true
parameters and asks how the estimates behave across repeated samples: bias and
root mean squared error of the posterior mean, and the coverage of 90%
credible intervals (which should be close to 90% when the priors are weak
relative to the data). Each design was replicated 200 times with 10 periods
on rook grids of $N = 100$ or 400 units.

```{r}
mc_tab <- mc[, c("design", "parameter", "true", "bias", "rmse", "cover90", "width")]
knitr::kable(mc_tab, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("design", "parameter", "true", "bias", "RMSE",
                           "90% coverage", "interval width"))
```

The static designs (binary SAR at $N = 100$ and 400, ordered SAR with four
categories) show biases of at most 0.02 and coverage between 0.88 and 0.92,
including for the total impact of $x_1$ (`impact_x1`), which is compared with
its true value computed from the true parameters. Quadrupling $N$ halves
the RMSE and interval widths, as it should.

The dynamic designs (`dyn_*`) use one data-generating process, with state
dependence ($\gamma = 0.8$, `lag_y`) and random effects
($\sigma_\alpha = 0.8$), and fit three models to it. The Wooldridge
random-effects model recovers $\gamma$ (bias 0.01, coverage 0.93). The pooled
dynamic model attributes the heterogeneity to state dependence: $\gamma$ is
overstated by 0.31 and the slopes are biased towards zero, so its intervals
almost never cover the truth. The static random-effects model, which
leaves out the lag, still estimates the slopes and $\rho$ well. See
`vignette("dynamics")`.

### The Wang and Kockelman simulation

Wang and Kockelman (2009) introduced the dynamic spatial ordered probit with
latent AR(1) dynamics and spatially autocorrelated effects, and evaluated it
on simulated data:

- three categories (thresholds 0 and 2.1) and four uniform regressors with
  $\beta = (-1.7, 2, 1, 0.5)$, over 8 periods;
- latent persistence $\lambda \in \{0.1, 0.5, 0.9\}$ crossed with spatial
  dependence of the effects $\rho \in \{0.1, 0.6, 0.7, 0.9\}$;
- 50 data sets per cell.

We repeated this design with `psoprobit(model = "none", effects =
"spatial_random", dynamic = psp_dynamic(latent = TRUE))`. Their $\lambda$ is
our `lag_z`, their $\rho$ our `phi`, and their $\sigma^2$ our
$\sigma_\alpha^2$. Three adaptations were needed:

- **Units.** Each of the 300 units has its own effect, on a 15 × 20 queen
  grid. This is a case their model allows; their own study used 30 regions of
  10 individuals.
- **Error variances.** All are equal to one, where theirs vary by region.
- **Thresholds.** Their thresholds are computed from our intercept and
  cut-point, so that the two sets of estimates are directly comparable.

We ran 2 chains of 15,000 draws after 5,000 of warm-up for each fit, where they
used one chain of 2,000.

```{r}
wk <- read.csv("validation-wk.csv")
cells <- unique(wk[, c("lambda", "rho")])
wk_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(cells)), function(k) {
  x <- wk[wk$lambda == cells$lambda[k] & wk$rho == cells$rho[k], ]
  g <- function(p, col) x[x$parameter == p, col]
  sl <- x[x$parameter %in% c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x4"), ]
  data.frame(lambda = cells$lambda[k], rho = cells$rho[k],
             lambda_psp = g("lambda", "mean"), lambda_wk = g("lambda", "paper"),
             rho_psp = g("rho", "mean"), rho_wk = g("rho", "paper"),
             sigma2_psp = g("sigma2", "mean"), sigma2_wk = g("sigma2", "paper"),
             slope_bias_psp = max(abs(sl$mean - sl$true)),
             slope_bias_wk = max(abs(sl$paper - sl$true)),
             cover90 = mean(x$cover90), rhat = g("x1", "rhat_share_1.05"))
}))
knitr::kable(wk_tab, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("&lambda;", "&rho;", "&lambda;: ours", "&lambda;: W&amp;K",
                           "&rho;: ours", "&rho;: W&amp;K", "&sigma;&sup2;: ours",
                           "&sigma;&sup2;: W&amp;K", "max slope bias: ours",
                           "max slope bias: W&amp;K", "90% coverage",
                           "share R-hat &ge; 1.05"))
```

The columns give the averages of the posterior means over the 50 data sets
(true $\sigma^2 = 1$), the largest absolute bias of the four slopes, the 90%
coverage averaged over all nine parameters, and the share of fits whose
largest $\hat R$ is at least 1.05. The full table, with RMSEs and the
thresholds, is in `validation/wang_kockelman/results/`.

Our estimates are close to the truth in every cell: overall 90% coverage is
`r round(mean(wk$cover90), 2)`, and the largest average bias of any
parameter is `r round(max(abs(wk$mean - wk$true)), 2)`. The paper's estimates
drift with $\lambda$ and $\rho$: $\sigma^2$ up to 1.8, and $\rho$ understated
when it is small. Their heteroskedastic design and shorter chains differ from
ours, so this does not locate the source of their bias.

When $\rho = 0.9$, two thirds to seven tenths of the fits still have
$\hat R \geq 1.05$ at our chain length. The effects are then nearly a common
level shared by all units, which trades off against the intercept, so the
thresholds (not the slopes) mix slowly. Their RMSE is 0.5 to 0.7, against 0.3
or less elsewhere. As
`?psprobit` advises, strongly autocorrelated effects need longer chains.

## 4. Cross-checks against other packages

Where another implementation of the same model exists, the posteriors should
agree up to Monte Carlo error.

- **`MCMCpack::MCMCoprobit`** (non-spatial pooled ordered probit, $N = 300$,
  $T = 4$, $J = 4$): every posterior mean agrees within 0.03 posterior
  standard deviations, and the posterior standard deviations agree within 2%.
- **`spatialprobit::sarprobit`** on its Katrina data (a cross-section of 673
  firms, pooled SAR probit, near-diffuse priors): the posterior means agree
  within 0.65 posterior standard deviations for all ten parameters, with
  `spatialprobit` started from good values (its defaults fail on these data).
  Given the SBC result above, exact agreement is not expected.
  `panelspatialprobit` was about 9 times faster.
- **`spatialprobit::sarorderedprobit`** (simulated pooled SAR ordered probit,
  20 × 20 grid, $T = 1$, $J = 4$, near-diffuse priors): every posterior mean
  agrees within 0.08 posterior standard deviations. The cut-points of
  `spatialprobit` mix slowly: an effective sample size of about 400 from
  200,000 draws, against 6,000–7,000 here from 32,000 draws, which took 1.3 s
  instead of 4 minutes.

## 5. Speed and mixing

Correctness is only useful if the sampler is fast enough to run long
chains. The table below gives the time per iteration and the effective sample
size per second for three random-effects models with five regressors, each
fitted with one chain on one core of an Intel Core i7-4790K: 10,000
iterations (half warm-up) at $N = 1{,}000$, and 2,000 at $N = 10{,}000$. The
effective sample size per second divides the bulk ESS by the whole run time,
including warm-up and the log-determinant grid; the range is over the
parameters, and the last column names the slowest one. The short chains at
$N = 10{,}000$ make those figures a rough guide.

```{r}
model_names <- c(sar_binary = "SAR probit", sar_ordered = "SAR ordered probit (J = 4)",
                 sem_binary = "SEM probit")
bench_tab <- data.frame(
  model = model_names[bench$design], N = format(bench$N, big.mark = ","), T = bench$T,
  ms = bench$ms_per_iter,
  ess = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", bench$ess_per_sec_min, bench$ess_per_sec_max),
  slowest = bench$slowest)
knitr::kable(bench_tab, row.names = FALSE, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("model", "N", "T", "ms per iteration", "ESS per second",
                           "slowest parameter"))
```

The ordered model costs about a quarter more per iteration than the binary
one, mainly for the cut-point updates. The SEM model costs about 1.8 times as
much, mainly because the precision of the random effects
depends on $\lambda$ and must be factorised again in every iteration. At
$N = 10{,}000$ and $T = 20$ (200,000 observations), 10,000 iterations take
about `r round(10000 * bench$ms_per_iter[bench$N == 10000 & bench$design == "sar_binary"] / 6e4, 1)`
minutes for the SAR probit and
`r round(10000 * bench$ms_per_iter[bench$N == 10000 & bench$design == "sem_binary"] / 6e4, 1)`
minutes for the SEM probit. The script is `validation/bench/bench_models.R`.

### Cut-points

In ordered models the cut-points are the hardest parameters to sample. The
Albert–Chib step draws each cut-point between the latent values of the
neighbouring categories, which pin it down tightly when there are many
observations, so it moves very little per iteration. The default sampler
adds a transformation move that shifts the cut-points and the latent values
together (`?psp_control`, `cutpoint_sampler`). The table compares the two on
ordered SAR random-effects models with $N = 400$ and $T = 5$, with $J = 3$
and $J = 5$ categories (four chains of 3,000 draws after 1,000 of warm-up;
the ratio is the ESS per second of the default sampler over that of the
Albert–Chib step alone).

```{r}
knitr::kable(data.frame(J = sub("J", "", cuts$design), cuts[, -1]), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("J", "parameter", "ESS (default)", "ESS (Albert-Chib)",
                           "ESS/s (default)", "ESS/s (Albert-Chib)", "ratio"))
```

```{r}
cut_rows <- grepl("^cut", cuts$parameter)
other <- cuts$ratio[!cut_rows]
```

For the interior cut-points with $J = 5$ the move raises the ESS per second
`r round(min(cuts$ratio[cut_rows & cuts$design == "J5" & cuts$ratio > 10]))`- to
`r round(max(cuts$ratio[cut_rows]))`-fold; the last cut-point already mixes
well under the Albert–Chib step, so it gains little. With $J = 3$ the gain is
`r cuts$ratio[cut_rows & cuts$design == "J3"]`-fold. The other parameters
change little (ratios `r min(other)` to `r max(other)`): the move adds about
15% to the time per iteration, and the rest of the spread is probably Monte
Carlo noise in the ESS estimates. The script is
`validation/bench/bench_cutpoints.R`.

arXiv:1804.06788.

and methods. *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 103, 790–796.

Wang, X. and Kockelman, K. M. (2009). Bayesian inference for ordered
response data with a dynamic spatial-ordered probit model. *Journal of
Regional Science* 49, 877–913.

Wilhelm, S. and de Matos, M. G. (2013). Estimating spatial probit models in R.
*The R Journal* 5(1), 130–143.
